newsitem.title: THAILAND: INTERVIEW-General Finance to switch focus.
newsitem.headline: INTERVIEW-General Finance to switch focus.

text.p: Difficult lending conditions in Thailand will see General Finance and Securities Plc place greater emphasis on its fee-based and brokerage operations in 1997, a company executive said on Wednesday.

Bob McMillen, managing director of investment banking, said GF's priorities were maintaining loan portfolio quality, developing international securities trading links and boosting investment banking revenues.
"In this market, liquidity is important. Even more emphasis will be placed on debt collection as our loan growth is not going to be as strong," McMillen told Reuters in an interview.

An economic slowdown in Thailand -- which saw GDP growth slow to 6.7 percent in 1996, its lowest level for a decade -- and a slump in the property market restrict high-quality lending opportunities, he said.
"On the securities side, we believe now is the time to forge and strengthen international relationships," he added.
"I certainly hope securities will make a bigger contribution to the bottom line than they did last year," he said.
According to the Stock Exchange of Thailand, GF's market share of value of share transactions in 1996 was 2.19 percent.

The company's technical services agreement with regional merchant bank PrimeEast Capital Group was gaining momentum, and the establishment of an institutional sales desk in September boosted trading revenues in the last quarter of 1996, he said.
GF also places orders on the market for Deutsche Morgan Grenfell but was looking at bringing in others, McMillen said.

On the finance side, maintaining loan portfolio quality was a priority, McMillen said. GF was among Thailand's top 10 finance firm lenders in 1996 with loan book worth approximately 60 billion baht ($2.4 billion).
"We need to be conservative in our provisioning, we need to be conservative in our cash flow management and conservative in our lending policies," he said.
Some 180 million baht of loan loss provisioning during the first half of 1996 helped General Finance ride more difficult market conditions at the end of last year, McMillen said.
But the economic slowdown had squeezed many firms and offered the prospect of more merger and acquisition (M & A) activity this year, McMillen said.
"I believe this is the year for M & A's, everyone is hungry and all the foreigners are looking very seriously at it ... On investment banking we are looking for a pretty good year," he said.
"We are advising an applicant on a life insurance bid, we've got three or four substantial M & A projects in hand at the moment," he added.
GF is handling a 3.75 billion baht initial public offering (IPO) in a new bank, in which GF is the core shareholder, McMillen said. The IPO is expected before the year end.
But McMillen warned that loan write-offs would severely contract 1996 fourth quarter earnings in the finance and securities sector. Most firms will report later this month.

"Any good finance company will have very, very bad results for the last three months of last year. Why the hell would you worry about last year? Just write off everything you possibly can, so you start with a clean slate in 1997," he said.
